name: Braising & Stewing
summary: Low, slow, moist heat that turns tough, cheap cuts tender, in the oven, on the stove, or in a slow or pressure cooker.

sections.heading: Why low and slow
blocks: Hard-working muscles (shoulder, chuck, brisket, shanks, short ribs, thighs) are full of connective tissue (collagen) that makes them chewy when cooked quickly. Held around a gentle simmer for a few hours, collagen melts into gelatin: the meat turns tender and the liquid turns silky.
That's why braises go far past the usual doneness temperatures: tough cuts are ready when they're **fork-tender**, around 195–205°F (90–96°C), not at 145°F (63°C). They're safe long before that.

sections.heading: Braise or stew
blocks: A **braise** is large pieces (a pot roast, short ribs, chicken thighs) partly covered by liquid. A **stew** is smaller, even chunks fully covered. The method is the same.

items: Pat the meat dry, season it well, and brown it in batches in a heavy pot (a Dutch oven is ideal). Browning builds most of the flavor; don't crowd the pot.
Take the meat out, then soften onions, carrots, celery and garlic in the fat. Stir in tomato paste or spices for a minute.
Add liquid (stock, wine, beer, tomatoes) and scrape up the browned bits. For a braise, add enough to come about halfway up the meat; for a stew, just cover it.
Return the meat, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook gently: in a 300–325°F (150–160°C) oven, or on the stovetop at the lowest simmer. The oven heats more evenly and won't scorch the bottom.
Cook until a fork slides in and twists easily, usually 2–4 hours depending on the cut and size.
Skim off the fat, and simmer the liquid uncovered to thicken it if needed. Braises taste even better the next day.

blocks.text: Keep it at a bare simmer. A hard boil tightens the meat fibers and makes it stringy and dry, even though it's sitting in liquid.

rows: Brown the meat in a pan first for flavor. Use less liquid than on the stove: nothing evaporates. Don't start with frozen meat, which lingers too long in the danger zone.
About a third of the stovetop time
Brown on the sauté setting first. Needs a minimum amount of thin liquid to come to pressure; check the manual. Let pressure release naturally for meat, so it stays tender.
The most even heat and the best browning on top. Lid on, or slightly ajar to reduce the liquid.
